CBAM

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (UK & EU)

A Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism charges importers for the carbon in certain goods, so they pay the same carbon price as local producers. The EU's CBAM has charged since 1 January 2026. The UK's starts on 1 January 2027 and works differently: it's a tax collected by HMRC.

Draft guide. We're checking this page against official sources before launch. Always confirm with your regulator.

Step 1

Are you in scope?

You're probably in if…

  • EU: you import more than 50 tonnes a year of iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen or electricity into the EU, and need authorised declarant status
  • UK: you import aluminium, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen or iron and steel worth £50,000 or more over 12 months (or expect to within 30 days)

You're probably out if…

  • EU: importers under the 50-tonne annual threshold
  • UK: importers under £50,000 a year of CBAM goods. Glass and ceramics were dropped from the UK scope

Who regulates it: EU: national CBAM authorities and the Commission's CBAM Registry. UK: HM Revenue & Customs.

Step 2

Your yearly routine

  1. All yearCollect embedded-emissions data from your non-UK/EU suppliers
  2. EU · from Feb 2027Buy CBAM certificates on the central platform
  3. EU · 30 SepAnnual CBAM declaration and certificate surrender for last year's imports (moved from 31 May by the 2025 CBAM Omnibus)
  4. UK · 31 Jan 2028Register with HMRC if you became liable during 2027
  5. UK · 31 May 2028First return and payment, covering 2027 imports

Key facts

EU certificate price
Linked to the EU ETS auction price
Carbon paid abroad
Can be deducted from what you owe, if you can prove it
Default values
Used when suppliers can't give real data. Usually more expensive
UK first return
31 May 2028, covering 2027. Later returns come round more often, so check HMRC guidance
Practical tip

Start asking suppliers for installation-level emissions data now. Without it you pay on default values, which are set high on purpose.
